source_checks.quote: Replication of “Social identity contingencies: How diversity cues signal threat or safety for African Americans in mainstream institutions” by V Purdie-Vaughns, CM Steele, PG Davies, R Ditlmann, JR Crosby (2008, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology). Kathleen Schmidt kes7z@virginia.edu Introduction In their original paper “Social identity contingencies: How diversity cues signal threat or safety for African Americans in mainstream institutions,” Purdie-Vaughns, Steele, Davies, Ditlmann, and Crosby (2008) suggest that people belonging to a group that is vulnerable to prejudice are especially sensitive to social identity contingencies—the set of potential “judgments, stereotypes, opportunities, restrictions, and treatments” related to social identity in an environment (Purdie-Vaughns et al. 2008). The researchers suggest that a given setting can produce expectations about social contingencies that affect personal comfort in that setting. In this replication of Purdie-Vaughns et al. (2008), I sought to reproduce the methodology used in the original paper as exactly as possible.

source_checks.quote: Confirmatory analysis A 2 X 2 ANOVA revealed a main effect of motivation, F(1,116) = 71.06, p < .001, = .38, indicating that people told to adjust by a large amount adjusted more (M = .27, SD = .39) than people told to adjust by a small amount (M = -.27, SD = .32). There was also a main effect of anchor precision, F(1,116) = 6.28, p = .014, = .05, indicating that people given the round anchor adjusted more (M = .08, SD = .48) than people given the precise anchor (M = -.08, SD = .40). There was no interaction between motivation and precision, F < 1. Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt These findings represent a partial replication of Janiszewski and Uy (2008). The central claim of their paper – that anchor precision influences the degree of adjustment was supported. Additionally, these data replicated the main effect of motivation observed in their study. There was no evidence of the reported interaction.

source_checks.quote: Confirmatory analysis The data from 20 participants were analyzed in order to attempt to replicate the original authors’ primary finding that older children performed at above-chance levels on “where” trials, answering an average of 1.41 out of 2 trials correctly, t(31) = 3.23, prep = .97. In our replication study, a one-sample t-test showed no such trend, M = 0.625, t(7) = -1.426, p = .197. Younger children (M = .833) also did not perform at above-chance levels on “where” trials, t(11) = -.804, p = .438. Similarly, neither the older (M = 1.125) or younger (M = 1.08) group performed at above-chance levels on “there” trials, t(7) = .357, p = .732 and t(11) = .364, p = .723, respectively. At one point during the planning of this replication, independent measures t-tests comparing younger versus older students on the number of correct “where” trial and “there” trial responses had been identified as the key finding. These analyses also showed no differences between younger and older children on “where” trials, t(18) = .627, p = .539, nor on “there” trials, t(18) = -1.04, p = .918. Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt Unlike in Nurmsoo and Bloom (2008), the confirmatory analysis for the current replication attempt did not reveal above-chance performance by older children on “where” trials. Thus, it is clear that we failed to replicate the original study’s finding.

source_checks.quote: 4.2 Statistical results A robust ERN was observed (mean amplitude = 6.44µV; SEM = .73) which was similar in magnitude to the original study (see Figure 1). This difference between ERP amplitudes following errors vs. correct responses was significant (t(40) = 8.69, p < .01). An error potentiated startle response was also apparent (see Figure 2), the magni- tude of which corresponded closely with the original study (mean difference between error and correct trials = 2.44µV; SEM = 1.17). This effect was significant. Paired t tests found that startle magnitude was greater following errors than following either subtype of correct trial, whether predictable, t(40) = 3.51, p < .01, or unpredictable t(28) = 2.08, p < .05. The main finding of the original study, a correlation between ERN and EPS am- plitude, did not reach the threshold for significance in our replication: r = -.25, p = .11, one-tailed. The original study reported a significant correlation: r = -.38, p < .05, one-tailed.

source_checks.quote: Replication of “The sunny side of fairness: Preference for fairness activates reward circuitry (and disregarding unfairness activates self-control circuitry)” by G Tabibnia, AB Satpute, MD Lieberman (2008, Psychological Science) Anastasia Rigney Taru Flagan Jennifer Beer beerutexas@gmail.com Introduction In their original paper “The sunny side of fairness: Preference for fairness activates reward circuitry (and disregarding unfairness activates self-control circuitry,” Tabibnia, Satpute, and Lieberman (2008) discuss the difficulties in separating the desire for fairness from the desire for material gain in the context of economic decision making. Accordingly, there had been little research on whether fair proposals produce positive emotional response due to its inherent fairness regardless of material gain. The original authors suggest that ultimatum games that require bilateral bargaining allow these motives to be tested independently. In this replication of Tabibnia et al. (2008), we sought to reproduce the methodology used in the original paper. The present work was conducted as part of the Reproducibility Project: Psychology which asks volunteers to replicate the final study in their chosen paper. Therefore, this is a direct replication of Experiment 2.
